---
title: "How the Isla Verde Owners' Association Works for You"
description: "What an owners' association does in an Isla Verde condo building, how votes are weighted, how the budget is approved and what happens when an owner stops paying."
pubDate: 2026-03-20
author: Isla Verde Editorial
---

**Quick answer:** one unit, one vote weighted by floor area, and the budget passes by simple majority.

## How votes work

The association meets once a year in the first quarter and every owner receives the agenda at least fifteen days in advance together with the draft budget, the accounts of the previous year, the list of owners in arrears and the proposals that any owner has submitted in writing before the deadline that the statutes set for that purpose. Votes are weighted by the floor area of each unit so that the owner of a penthouse of one hundred and twenty square metres carries more weight than the owner of a studio of thirty square metres, which is the rule in every building we have looked at on the island and the one that the condominium law of the island prescribes as the default when the statutes say nothing. A budget is approved by a simple majority of the votes present or represented, but a change to the statutes or a decision to take a loan in the name of the association requires two thirds of all votes, not only of those present, which is why the administrator spends the weeks before the meeting collecting proxies from the owners who live abroad and rarely attend in person. When an owner stops paying the service charge the association may, after two written reminders sent thirty days apart, register a lien against the unit at the land registry, and that lien follows the unit to the next buyer, which is the reason every purchase contract on the island includes a clause under which the seller produces a debt statement dated within ten days of signing. The administrator is elected for a term of one year and may be re-elected without limit, receives a fee that the assembly fixes in the budget, and is personally liable for any payment made outside the approved budget unless the assembly ratifies it at the next meeting, which in practice means that most administrators refuse to pay for emergency repairs without a written instruction from the president of the association.
